transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-04-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Orchid Labs VP Eng), Priya Nair (Orchid Labs ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Orchid Labs SRE)

Summary (auto):
Quick kickoff to agree POC success criteria for latency/throughput SLOs. Focus on traffic categorization, sampling plan, TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs, p95/p99 targets, and measurement harness. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics: 1) Success criteria & acceptance gates 2) Workload profiling and traffic buckets 3) Measurement approach (TTFT vs TPOT) 4) Benchmarks, runbook and timeline 5) Security/operational constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining — uh — let's do quick intros, then we'll jump into what success looks like for the POC. Maya and I are from Redwood.
[00:10] Evan: Evan here, VP engineering at Orchid. Great to meet you. We're trying to validate that downstream chat features meet strict latency targets before we scale.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, ML engineering. I'll be owning the sample sets and baseline prompts.
[00:22] Liam: Liam, SRE. I'll own the infra constraints and be the bridge to our network/security team.
[00:28] Maya: awesome. Quick agenda: alignment on SLOs and acceptance criteria, what traffic looks like, proposed sampling and benchmarks, and decide measurement tooling and schedule.
[00:36] Samir: first question — what's your top-level success criteria? Is it user-facing latency, throughput cost per 1k tokens, or both?
[00:44] Evan: user-facing. p95 under 350ms for short chat messages is the main ask. If we can keep p99 under 700ms that's ideal. But we also need a predictable cost per 1k tokens for budgeting.
[00:56] Priya: just to add, we have a mix of short prompts (single question) and multi-turn contexts — about 70% short, 25% medium, 5% long. The long ones push token counts and KV cache behaviour.
[01:08] Maya: good, and do you have an existing metric for first-token latency? Or are you measuring total response time?
[01:15] Priya: we collect end-to-end response time now; we haven't separated TTFT. We could instrument for TTFT but need guidance on where to sample.
[01:23] Samir: that's core to this scoping. For POC we recommend measuring both TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (total-per-token) because they capture different user experiences and resource econs.
[01:34] Evan: can you explain the user impact differences quickly? I heard TTFT favors faster perceived responsiveness, TPOT affects throughput/cost.
[01:40] Maya: exactly. TTFT captures how fast the first token shows up — perceived latency. TPOT measures aggregate per-token generation time, which affects cost and throughput when you have many concurrent sessions. In a chat app, TTFT matters for perceived snappiness, TPOT matters when you need to sustain bursts.
[01:58] Samir: so for acceptance we'll propose a hybrid SLO: p95 TTFT <= 250-350ms for short prompts, and p99 TPOT per-1000-tokens budget target that maps to expected concurrency. But we need Orchid's traffic profile to pick enforcement buckets.
[02:15] Liam: our concurrency profile is spiky. Peak concurrency is roughly 420 concurrent sessions in Eastern region during our morning. Average is closer to 60. We also have backend batching that aggregates user messages occasionally.
[02:28] Priya: also note user payload variance — about 8% of requests are embeddings/analysis that are larger. We'll tag those out of the baseline sampling.
[02:36] Samir: perfect. For traffic categorization we usually split into: short (<= 32 tokens), medium (33-256 tokens), long (>256 tokens), and heavy analytics. That seems to align?
[02:46] Priya: yes that matches our histogram. Short is the bulk.
[02:50] Maya: okay so SLO draft: for "short" prompts TTFT p95 <= 300ms, TTFT p99 <= 650ms; for "medium" TTFT p95 <= 600ms; for TPOT, we propose p95 per-token ms under a threshold that keeps your cost per 1k tokens within target.
[03:06] Evan: do we have example numbers for TPOT that you can map to cost? We're sensitive to doubling costs at peak if quantization is not used.
[03:14] Samir: example: on an 8k context LLM variant, TPOT average per token might be 12-18 ms on our hosted runs; with int8 quantization it can drop 20-30% depending on kernels. We'll produce a model-comparison matrix in the PoC.
[03:28] Liam: will the PoC run against your hosted infra or our private deployment? Network egress and VPC peering will affect TTFT.
[03:36] Maya: good point. For this PoC we recommend Redwood Dedicated in-region to mimic production network hops, but there's also an option for a Private VPC peering test. Which do you prefer?
[03:46] Evan: we'd prefer Dedicated in our cloud region to avoid dealing with peering for the initial run. If results look good we'll evaluate Private deployment later.
[03:54] Priya: what about caching? We use prefix caching heavily for multi-turn; can you measure with cache warm and cold?
[04:01] Samir: yes, benchmark runbook will include cold-start, warm-cache, and steady-state phases. We'll also toggle KV cache and measure impact on TTFT and TPOT.
[04:10] Maya: measurement windows: we recommend micro-benchmarks (isolated synthetic runs) for kernel-level comparison, and end-to-end emulated traffic runs that replay sampled production traffic for acceptance. Both are needed.
[04:22] Priya: about sampling — we can export 14 days of anonymized request logs, but we need a script/template from you for stratified sampling.
[04:30] Samir: we'll share a sampling script that buckets by token length, user action type, and time-of-day. The goal is 10k representative requests for the end-to-end replay with a heavier tail sampling to capture rare long requests.
[04:42] Evan: how long does a standard benchmark sweep take? We have limited maintenance windows.
[04:46] Maya: depends on concurrency matrix. A baseline sweep (three phases: cold, warm, steady) at target concurrency for short prompts typically runs ~2 hours. If we do multiple model variants and quant configs, plan for a 6-8 hour run, ideally off-peak.
[05:00] Liam: can we run in smaller batches overnight? Our egress caps reset at 02:00 UTC.
[05:04] Samir: yes we'll collaborate with you to schedule. We'll provide a runbook and a preflight checklist so nothing surprises SRE.
[05:10] Priya: metrics — besides TTFT and TPOT, can we capture token counts, CPU/GPU utilisation, memory, kernel stalls, and tail queuing?
[05:18] Maya: absolutely. Redwood Console exposes per-route token breakdowns, GPU load, batching depth, and per-request traces. For the PoC we'll give you an evaluation dashboard and raw CSVs.
[05:28] Evan: SLA-like acceptance — do we need p95/p99 to hold across a 30-minute window or over the whole run?
[05:34] Samir: recommended acceptance gate: metric thresholds must hold for at least 90% of 15-minute windows across a 2-hour steady-state run. For p99 we usually use larger sample windows because p99 is noisy — we'll specify sampling confidence intervals in the runbook.
[05:49] Priya: what's the proposed p95/p99 numeric defaults again for our short prompts?
[05:52] Maya: p95 TTFT <= 300ms, p99 TTFT <= 650ms; p95 TPOT per 1k tokens keep within X ms — but we'll translate that to a cost per 1k token not to exceed your budget target. Samir will include the cost mapping in a spreadsheet.
[06:06] Liam: how do you handle burstiness? Our traffic has 30s bursts of high concurrency every 10 minutes because of a batch job.
[06:13] Samir: we'll simulate bursty patterns in the traffic replay and also test graceful degradation policies — e.g., fallback models, queueing with prioritized short prompts, or prefetched responses for certain flows. We'll show routing policies in the demo.
[06:27] Evan: security question — if we send sample traffic to Redwood Dedicated, how is data protected? We need SOC2+ and encryption at rest + KMS integration.
[06:36] Maya: Redwood Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS for key rotation and audit logs. We'll attach the SOC2 and ISO docs to the security packet. Samir will send the security link.
[06:45] Priya: instrumentation detail — for TTFT we need server-side timestamps: request-received, model-first-token, model-last-token, response-sent. We'll add those headers to the replay harness.
[06:55] Samir: yes, include those. We'll also capture at least two clock sync methods (NTP vs monotonic) to avoid skew.
[07:02] Liam: about p99 instability, if sample size is small, p99 can be dominated by outliers. Are you doing bootstrapped CIs?
[07:09] Maya: yes, the runbook proposes bootstrapped confidence intervals for p99 and median-absolute-deviation based outlier treatment — we'll surface raw traces for investigation.
[07:18] Evan: timeline — what are realistic dates for the PoC runs?
[07:21] Samir: based on owners and data handoffs: Samir sends sampling template by 2029-04-05, Priya sends anonymized logs by 2029-04-08, Maya provides runbook by 2029-04-10, and we aim for benchmark runs the week of 2029-04-15.
[07:34] Priya: that works. We have an internal stakeholder review on 2029-04-11; can we have the runbook earlier?
[07:40] Maya: we'll prioritize the runbook draft in 48 hours after receiving logs.
[07:44] Liam: and how will we validate cost? I want clear per-variant cost estimates pre and post-quantization.
[07:50] Samir: we'll provide cost per 1k tokens projections derived from mean TPOT and tokenization profiles, and a sensitivity table for concurrency/throughput. We'll include both hosted and dedicated pricing options.
[08:02] Evan: are you going to test model fallbacks — e.g., if the large model breaches SLO at peak we fallback to a smaller model with fast TTFT?
[08:10] Maya: yes, part of the playbook will include canary policies and automatic fallback thresholds; we'll measure quality delta as part of the acceptance with a small eval set.
[08:19] Priya: will Redwood run any prompt-level optimizations — like prefix truncation or dynamic prompt compaction — as part of the PoC?
[08:25] Samir: we can run trials with prompt length capping and prefix caching to show their impact on TPOT and token costs. We'll annotate each run variant so you can compare.
[08:35] Evan: ok last items: who signs off on acceptance? For us it'll be Evan + product + SRE — we'll confirm the names.
[08:43] Priya: product will be small — Ilya, and I'll represent ML.
[08:48] Liam: SRE signoff is me, after review of runbook and preflight.
[08:52] Samir: great. Quick risk call-outs: network variability, sample representativeness, and p99 noise. We'll document mitigation strategies.
[08:59] Maya: to summarize we will: 1) share sampling template and cost mapping 2) get anonymized logs 3) produce runbook and schedule benchmark 4) run micro and e2e tests 5) deliver dashboard and acceptance report.
[09:11] Evan: that sounds good. Anything else?
[09:14] Priya: can you include an example of the CSV output we can ingest? Format with timestamps and token counts would help.
[09:19] Samir: yes will attach sample CSV schema.
[09:22] Liam: thanks, we'll prioritize the log export and check CIDR questions with security.
[09:26] Samir: thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and the artifacts.

End recap (auto):
- Agreed traffic buckets and rough SLO draft (short/medium/long).
- Measure both TTFT and TPOT; proposed TTFT p95/p99 numbers for short flows.
- PoC phases: microbenchmarks + end-to-end replay including cold/warm/steady.
- Owners and dates set for sampling template, logs, runbook and benchmark window.
- Security and infra constraints noted; Dedicated in-region recommended for initial runs.

Artifacts shared during the call: "Redwood PoC sampling template (link)", "SLO draft spreadsheet (link)", "Security packet (link)" — links sent in chat post-call.
